body:
Location and date

Adalaj ni Vav, also known as Rudabai Stepwell, is situated at Adalaj in present-day Gandhinagar district, north of Ahmedabad.

It belongs to the late 15th century and is generally dated to 1499 CE in official tourism descriptions. Some historical references use 1498 CE when interpreting its inscription and calendar date. The important historical identification is its construction around 1498–1499 during the Gujarat Sultanate period.

The stepwell is associated with Queen Rudabai, also called Rooda, wife of the Vaghela chief Virsinh or Veer Singh.

It was constructed during the reign of Sultan Mahmud Begada. However, the association with his reign must not be confused with the identity of the principal patron: the stepwell is attributed to Rudabai.

Remember the patron

Adalaj ni Vav is associated with Queen Rudabai, wife of the Vaghela chief Virsinh. Mahmud Begada was the contemporary Sultan of Gujarat, not the queen's husband.

Historical evidence and popular traditions

A Sanskrit inscription at the monument records information about Rudabai and her family. It is important evidence for establishing the patronage of the stepwell.

Popular narratives also describe conflicts between Virsinh and Mahmud Begada, followed by events involving the queen and the completion of the structure. These stories form part of the site's local tradition, but their dramatic details should not be treated as independently established historical facts.

Architectural arrangement

Adalaj ni Vav is a 5-storey stepwell constructed largely from stone. Like other substantial Gujarat vavs, it contains stairways, pillared spaces and a deeper well area.

Its distinctive features include:

  • 3 entrances providing access to the upper underground gallery.
  • An important octagonal opening above the entrance-level space.
  • Descending steps leading towards the lower well.
  • Pillars and beams supporting the multi-storeyed structure.
  • Carved architectural surfaces containing religious and ornamental motifs.

The main arrangement follows a north–south axis, with the well towards the northern end and the principal approach from the south.

Why does the octagonal opening matter?

The opening above the upper landing admits light and air into the underground structure. This makes the space more usable while preserving shaded areas below.

The geometry of the opening also contributes to the monument's recognizable architectural character.

Water and public life

Adalaj ni Vav provided access to water and offered resting space to travellers, merchants and local residents. Its multi-level galleries made it more than a simple well.

The monument also demonstrates how a major public water structure could become a setting for religious symbolism and elaborate artistic expression.

Prelims focus

  • Location: Adalaj, Gandhinagar district, Gujarat.
  • Date: Commonly 1499 CE; some historical accounts use 1498 CE.
  • Patron: Queen Rudabai, wife of Vaghela chief Virsinh.
  • Period: Reign of Mahmud Begada.
  • Architecture: 5 storeys, 3 entrances and an octagonal opening.
  • Trap: Rudabai was the patron; Mahmud Begada was the ruling Sultan during the period.

[References: Government of India, India Cine Hub, Adalaj Ni Vaav, historical and architectural description, consulted 23 November 2026; Ahmedabad District Administration, Government of Gujarat, Adalaj Vav, historical description, consulted 23 November 2026; Gujarat Tourism, Adalaj ni Vav, About the Location, consulted 23 November 2026; Ministry of Tourism, Utsav Portal, Heritage Festival at Adalaj ni Vav, site description, consulted 23 November 2026; Studies in Gujarat History, Adalaj Ni Vav, transcription and discussion of the Sanskrit inscription, consulted 23 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: The distinctive entrances, octagonal opening and descending storeys of Adalaj ni Vav.

title: Adalaj ni Vav: Queen Rudabai, Historical Patronage and Architectural Design

body:
A combination of architectural traditions

Adalaj ni Vav is an important example of the Indo-Islamic architectural synthesis that developed in Gujarat during the Sultanate period.

Its building methods and decoration reflect the continuation of established western Indian stone-carving traditions alongside architectural and ornamental influences associated with the Gujarat Sultanate.

These traditions developed through the work of local craftsmen and their patrons. The result is not an entirely Islamic structure replacing an earlier Hindu one, but a monument that incorporates elements of different artistic traditions.

Important decorative features

Ami Khumbor

The Ami Khumbor is a carved representation of an auspicious vessel associated with the water of life. It expresses ideas of abundance, nourishment and well-being.

Its presence in a water monument is especially meaningful because the stepwell itself provided access to an essential natural resource.

Kalpavriksha

The Kalpavriksha is the wish-fulfilling tree of Indian religious tradition. Its representation expresses auspiciousness, prosperity and the fulfilment of wishes.

At Adalaj, the representation is associated with the intricate carving of its architectural surfaces.

Navagraha

A carved panel depicts the Navagraha, the 9 celestial influences of traditional Indian religious astronomy and astrology.

Local belief associates the representation with protection from inauspicious influences. This is a statement about religious belief, not a scientifically established protective property of the carving.

Other carved subjects

The monument also contains floral and geometric ornament, mythological subjects and scenes associated with village life.

These different images show that the decorative programme was not limited to a single religious theme.

Understanding the architectural combination

The monument's stone columns, beams and sculptural traditions have important connections with earlier western Indian architecture. At the same time, the decorative treatment and architectural composition reflect the broader cultural setting of the Gujarat Sultanate.

The combination of local forms with Sultanate-period influences is why Adalaj is commonly described as an Indo-Islamic monument.

Do not confuse a decorative symbol with the patron

The presence of Hindu or Jain-associated imagery does not by itself identify the ruler who commissioned a building. Patronage must be established through historical evidence, including inscriptions, rather than inferred only from the decoration.

How does Adalaj differ from Rani-ki-Vav?

Both monuments combine access to water with architectural and artistic excellence. However, their historical settings and dominant architectural descriptions differ.

  • Rani-ki-Vav: An 11th-century Solanki memorial stepwell especially associated with Maru-Gurjara architecture and an extensive Vaishnava sculptural programme.
  • Adalaj ni Vav: A late-15th-century stepwell associated with Rudabai and recognized for its combination of western Indian and Gujarat Sultanate architectural influences.

Prelims focus

  • Adalaj is an important example of Indo-Islamic architectural synthesis in Gujarat.
  • Ami Khumbor: An auspicious vessel associated with the water of life.
  • Kalpavriksha: The wish-fulfilling tree.
  • Navagraha: The traditional group of 9 celestial influences.
  • Floral, geometric, mythological and village-life scenes occur in its decoration.
  • Trap: Maru-Gurjara is particularly associated with Rani-ki-Vav, while Indo-Islamic synthesis is a defining description of Adalaj ni Vav.

[References: Gujarat Tourism, Adalaj ni Vav, About the Location, including the descriptions of Ami Khumbor, Kalpavriksha and Navagraha, consulted 23 November 2026; Ahmedabad District Administration, Government of Gujarat, Places of Interest, Adalaj Stepwell, consulted 23 November 2026; Government of India, India Cine Hub, Adalaj Ni Vaav, historical description, consulted 23 November 2026; NCERT, Living Craft Traditions of India, Class 11, Stone, printed pp. 27–29.]

body:
Bai Harir ni Vav or Dada Harir Stepwell

Bai Harir ni Vav, also known as Dada Harir ni Vav, is located in the Asarwa area of Ahmedabad.

It belongs to the late 15th century and is associated with Dhai Harir or Bai Harir Sultani, a woman connected with the royal household of Sultan Mahmud Begada.

The Sanskrit inscription at the monument is commonly dated to 1499 CE. Historical accounts of its Arabic and Sanskrit inscriptions have produced some differences in reported dates, but the late-15th-century identification and association with Bai Harir are well established.

The stepwell contains 5 descending storeys, carved stone columns and an octagonal arrangement near the upper part of the structure. It provided access to water and created shaded spaces for public use.

Its association with a female patron is particularly important. Like Rani-ki-Vav and Adalaj, it demonstrates that women could commission major public water structures.

Distinguishing Bai Harir from Adalaj

Both structures belong to the late 15th century and have 5 descending storeys. Both are associated with the reign of Mahmud Begada. However, they are different monuments with different patrons.

  • Adalaj: Rudabai, wife of Virsinh; located in present-day Gandhinagar district.
  • Bai Harir: Bai Harir Sultani, associated with the Sultan's royal household; located at Asarwa in Ahmedabad.

Mata Bhavani ni Vav

Mata Bhavani ni Vav is another important stepwell in the Asarwa area of Ahmedabad.

Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation's heritage documentation describes it as an early stepwell dating to the 11th-century Solanki period.

Its architectural arrangement includes a long stepped passage descending through 3 storeys, with 3 open pavilions arranged along an east–west axis.

The pillars, brackets and beams demonstrate the decorative stone-building traditions associated with early western Indian stepwells.

The stepwell takes its present name from a shrine associated with Mata Bhavani. The name of the shrine should not be mistaken for the identity of a historically established individual patron.

Historical distinction

Mata Bhavani ni Vav is associated with the Solanki period, whereas Bai Harir ni Vav belongs to the later Gujarat Sultanate period. Both are located in the Asarwa area of Ahmedabad.

Amritvarshini Vav

Amritvarshini Vav, also called Panchkuva Stepwell or Katkhuni Vav, is located near Panchkuva in the historic walled city of Ahmedabad.

It dates to approximately 1723 CE, during the Mughal period in Gujarat. Its inscriptions are associated with the period of the provincial governor Haidar Quli Khan and his diwan, Raghunathdas.

Its most distinctive feature is an L-shaped plan. Unlike a long straight stepped corridor, the passage changes direction before reaching the deeper water structure.

It also incorporates arches and has a comparatively restrained decorative treatment. Its plan demonstrates that stepwell architecture could be adapted to different urban sites and historical building traditions.

Identifying the Ahmedabad examples

StepwellLocation and periodKey identification
Bai Harir ni VavAsarwa, Ahmedabad; late 15th centuryBai Harir Sultani; 5 storeys
Mata Bhavani ni VavAsarwa, Ahmedabad; 11th centurySolanki period; 3 storeys and 3 open pavilions
Amritvarshini VavPanchkuva, Ahmedabad; around 1723Distinctive L-shaped plan

Prelims focus

  • Bai Harir ni Vav is located at Asarwa and is associated with Bai Harir Sultani.
  • Bai Harir belongs to the late 15th century and has 5 storeys.
  • Mata Bhavani ni Vav is associated with the 11th-century Solanki period.
  • Mata Bhavani has 3 storeys and 3 open pavilions.
  • Amritvarshini Vav, near Panchkuva, is associated with 1723 CE and an L-shaped plan.
  • Trap: Bai Harir and Rudabai are different patrons associated with different stepwells.

[References: Gujarat Tourism, Bai Harir Ni Vav, About the Location and Brief History, consulted 23 November 2026; Government of India, Incredible India, Dada Harir Vav, historical description and inscription, consulted 23 November 2026; Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation, Heritage City, Mata Bhavani Vav, historical and architectural description, consulted 23 November 2026; Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation, Heritage City, Amritvarshini Vav, historical and architectural description, consulted 23 November 2026.]

body:
Rock-cut water structures at Uparkot

The stepwells at Uparkot Fort in Junagadh demonstrate a different approach to water architecture.

Many developed Gujarat vavs were constructed using masonry pillars, beams, walls and stairs. At Uparkot, important water structures were instead excavated substantially from the existing rock.

This difference is significant because a rock-cut structure is created principally by removing natural rock, whereas a masonry stepwell requires the construction and assembly of separate structural components.

Adi-Kadi Vav

Adi-Kadi Vav is a notable rock-cut stepwell within Uparkot Fort, Junagadh.

Gujarat Tourism dates it to the 15th century. A narrow descending staircase is cut into the rock and leads towards the well shaft.

The staircase is described as having approximately 120 steps.

Unlike the elaborate pillared galleries of Rani-ki-Vav, its most distinctive architectural quality is the direct excavation of the stairway and well access from hard rock.

Traditional stories associate its name with 2 women called Adi and Kadi. These stories belong to local folklore and should not be used as firm evidence for the identity of the monument's original builders.

Navghan Kuvo

Navghan Kuvo is another major historical water structure inside Uparkot Fort.

Its most distinctive feature is a spiralling staircase arranged around the well shaft. The structure combines excavation from rock with constructed architectural elements.

The availability of water within the fort was important during periods of siege, when access to external water sources could be interrupted.

Navghan Kuvo is considerably older than the 15th-century Adi-Kadi Vav, although published accounts differ regarding its precise construction date.

Uparkot identification

  • Adi-Kadi Vav: Rock-cut descending staircase leading towards a well.
  • Navghan Kuvo: Staircase spiralling around the well shaft.

Surya Kund at Modhera: a different water structure

The Surya Kund, also called Rama Kund, is situated in front of the Sun Temple at Modhera in Gujarat.

The Sun Temple belongs to the early 11th-century Solanki period and is associated with King Bhimdev I.

Surya Kund is a large rectangular stepped tank. Its descending steps create a geometric arrangement around the open water basin.

The steps contain 108 miniature shrines, demonstrating the close relationship between water structures and religious architecture.

The kund formed part of the temple's sacred architectural complex and was associated with ritual use of water.

Why Surya Kund is not the same as a vav

A conventional developed vav provides a stepped approach towards a deeper well shaft. Surya Kund is primarily an open rectangular stepped tank.

Both represent important Gujarat water architecture, but their arrangements and architectural functions differ.

The relationship between Modhera and Rani-ki-Vav

Both monuments belong to the broad cultural and architectural setting of Solanki-period Gujarat.

However, Rani-ki-Vav is an underground memorial stepwell, while Surya Kund forms part of a temple complex. The similarity in period and artistic tradition does not make them the same type of monument.

Prelims focus

  • Adi-Kadi Vav and Navghan Kuvo are located within Uparkot Fort at Junagadh.
  • Adi-Kadi Vav is associated with rock-cut construction and a staircase of approximately 120 steps.
  • Navghan Kuvo has a spiralling staircase around its well shaft.
  • Surya Kund is located at the Sun Temple, Modhera.
  • Surya Kund is a rectangular stepped tank with 108 miniature shrines.
  • Trap: Surya Kund is a stepped tank, not the same architectural form as Rani-ki-Vav or Adalaj ni Vav.

[References: Gujarat Tourism, Adi-Kadi Vav, About the Location, consulted 23 November 2026; Gujarat Tourism, Navghan Kuwo, About the Location, consulted 23 November 2026; Gujarat Tourism, Uparkot Fort, monument description, consulted 23 November 2026; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, chapter 6, Temple Architecture and Sculpture, West India, printed pp. 75–76; Gujarat Tourism, Modhera Sun Temple, description of Surya Kund, consulted 23 November 2026.]
